source_note: Every rule below is a single case study from one company, not a controlled multi-trial finding. Each is validated in its own context, not proven as a general law. Use the 'condition' field to check fit before applying. Where two rules contradict, that is not an error in this file — it means they assume opposite starting conditions. Check 'contradicts' before picking a lever.

PAYWALL-01.lever: Show an explicit day-by-day billing timeline during the trial, including the exact charge date.
PAYWALL-01.mechanism: Removes the fear of a surprise charge, which is often the real blocker, not the trial's value.
PAYWALL-01.condition: User has already agreed to start the trial. The friction is billing anxiety, not product doubt.
PAYWALL-01.evidence: Blinkist: +23% trial signups, -55% customer complaints, push opt-ins rose from 6% to 74%.

PAYWALL-02.lever: Offer the free trial only on the annual plan, or give annual a longer trial than monthly.
PAYWALL-02.mechanism: Makes annual feel like the safer, lower-risk option instead of the bigger commitment.
PAYWALL-02.condition: You want to nudge undecided users toward annual and can tolerate monthly users getting a worse or no trial.
PAYWALL-02.evidence: Moonly: +39% view-to-subscription conversion. Headspace: 7-day trial on monthly, 14-day on annual, double-digit conversion increase despite delaying revenue.

PAYWALL-03.lever: Single-tap trial start with gain-framed copy (e.g. "redeem your free 2 weeks"), skipping a second paywall/confirmation screen.
PAYWALL-03.mechanism: Fewer steps plus framing the trial as something being given, not something being asked for.
PAYWALL-03.condition: User already has enough context to decide without more selling on a second screen.

PAYWALL-04.lever: Default the paywall to showing only the yearly plan; put monthly behind a secondary "view all plans" link.
PAYWALL-04.mechanism: Removes the side-by-side comparison that lets users default to the cheaper, smaller commitment.
PAYWALL-04.condition: Same as PAYWALL-02 — you're optimizing for annual mix, and are OK with monthly users doing extra work to find their option.

PAYWALL-05.lever: Show the paywall immediately when the app is opened, before any feature use.
PAYWALL-05.mechanism: Works when the value prop is already understood from the app store listing or marketing, so there's nothing left to demonstrate.
PAYWALL-05.condition: The product's value is legible without hands-on use. If it isn't, this will read as an ambush.

PAYWALL-06.lever: Before asking for the trial, make the cost of inaction vivid — project a habit or behavior forward (e.g. lifetime hours lost) instead of only describing the product's benefit.
PAYWALL-06.mechanism: Creates a motivated moment, similar to why gym-membership commitment effects work, right before the ask.
PAYWALL-06.condition: Product addresses a habit or behavior the user already has some regret about (screen time, spending, etc.). Doesn't transfer to neutral utility products.
PAYWALL-06.evidence: Opal: trial-signup conversion rate went from 7% to 17% across iterations.

PAYWALL-07.lever: Require a credit card for the trial instead of running freemium or a no-card trial.
PAYWALL-07.mechanism: Filters for intent and reduces low-value support load, at the cost of top-of-funnel volume.
PAYWALL-07.condition: Support cost or low-intent signups are an actual measured problem, and you're willing to trade volume for conversion rate. Reported lift did not include funnel-volume data — check that before copying this.
PAYWALL-07.evidence: Outseta: 35% trial-to-paid conversion vs. 7.25% on freemium (4-5x).

PAYWALL-08.lever: Let premium content play for a short window (e.g. 10 seconds) before the paywall interrupts, instead of gating it up front.
PAYWALL-08.mechanism: Value has to be tasted to be believed; gating first never lets the user find out what they'd be paying for.
PAYWALL-08.condition: The product's value is experiential and hard to convey in text or a screenshot (video, audio, live content).
PAYWALL-08.evidence: PepTalk: conversion with the taste-first variant "significantly" beat the gate-first variant.

PAYWALL-09.lever: Send a reminder (email/push) a few days before the trial ends.
PAYWALL-09.mechanism: Surfaces value again right before the decision point and reduces "I forgot I was in a trial" cancellations, without adding a hard sell.
PAYWALL-09.condition: Standard trial-to-paid transition where users may simply lose track of the date.
PAYWALL-09.evidence: Shaw Academy: +14% sales at reported 99%+ significance, without a matching rise in cancellations.

PAYWALL-10.lever: Add a badge or explicit framing ("free during the month", "save 60%") to an offer that isn't otherwise changing.
PAYWALL-10.mechanism: Same offer, clearer framing of what's being gained — badges make an existing deal legible instead of buried in body copy.
PAYWALL-10.condition: The underlying offer is already good; the problem is presentation, not substance.

PAYWALL-11.lever: Replace marketing copy on the paywall with a real user review and star rating.
PAYWALL-11.mechanism: Peer proof outweighs brand copy when the audience is skeptical of self-promotion.
PAYWALL-11.condition: You have a genuinely strong review to use, and the audience is more swayed by peers than by the brand's own voice.

PAYWALL-12.lever: Tune paywall visuals and copy to the audience's specific identity or emotional register, not generic feature-benefit language.
PAYWALL-12.mechanism: Identity-driven audiences respond to belonging and cause more than to a features list.
PAYWALL-12.condition: The audience has a strong shared identity (a diaspora publication, a niche community, a cause). This is an audience-fit result, not a general "emotion beats benefits" law — don't apply it to audiences without that shared identity.
PAYWALL-12.evidence: Neos Kosmos: image test +13%, tone-of-voice test ("support our work" vs. benefit-listing) +16%.

CHECKOUT-01.lever: Remove mandatory account creation at checkout; ask only name and email, replace password creation with a reset-link flow.
CHECKOUT-01.mechanism: Cuts the last blocker when purchase intent is already high.
CHECKOUT-01.condition: User has already committed to the purchase decision (picked the item/room/service); account creation is the only remaining step, not the trust-builder.

CHECKOUT-02.lever: Show a single point-estimate price instead of a range.
CHECKOUT-02.mechanism: Users anchor to the top of a displayed range and hesitate; a single number reads as more trustworthy even if less "technically accurate."
CHECKOUT-02.condition: Trust in the number matters more to the user than precision about variability.
CHECKOUT-02.evidence: Uber: double-digit increase in rides per user.

CHECKOUT-03.lever: Restate an existing incentive (best-price guarantee, free-shipping threshold, returns policy) at the actual decision point, not just on a policy page.
CHECKOUT-03.mechanism: Users don't reread policy pages; repeating the incentive where the decision is being made changes the outcome even though nothing about the offer changed.
CHECKOUT-03.condition: The incentive already exists and is real — this is a visibility fix, not a new offer.
CHECKOUT-03.evidence: Buyagift: +9.6% sales. Clarks: +2.6% conversions. T.M. Lewin: +50% conversion rate, +7% monthly sales.

CHECKOUT-04.lever: Add short, benefit-focused copy (and/or top reviews) near the top of the product page.
CHECKOUT-04.mechanism: High-traffic, low-conversion pages often lead with generic description instead of the reason to buy.
CHECKOUT-04.condition: Traffic is not the problem; the page currently under-sells before the fold.
CHECKOUT-04.evidence: Goldelucks: +31.6% orders, +66.2% order revenue. Hannah & Henry (AI-generated version): +45.7% sales.

CHECKOUT-05.lever: Offer cart abandoners a limited-time discount with a countdown timer.
CHECKOUT-05.mechanism: Reactivates intent that was already warm (they added to cart), rather than manufacturing urgency from nothing.
CHECKOUT-05.condition: Target users showed real prior intent (cart add), not cold traffic.

CHECKOUT-06.lever: Add a values/storytelling panel (craftsmanship, sustainability, origin) to the product page.
CHECKOUT-06.mechanism: Differentiates on story where the product is premium or handmade and competes against commodity alternatives.
CHECKOUT-06.condition: Brand positioning already depends on craft/values, not just price or convenience.
CHECKOUT-06.evidence: Beckett Simonon: +5% sales, 237% annualized ROI on the panel.

CHECKOUT-07.lever: Before testing any lever, verify the current flow isn't just broken or confusing.
CHECKOUT-07.mechanism: Some "conversion wins" are bug fixes wearing a growth-hack costume — clarifying real UI confusion isn't a psychological lever, it's cleanup.
CHECKOUT-07.condition: Always check this first, especially when complaint volume or confused-user reports exist.
CHECKOUT-07.evidence: Chick-fil-A: fixed a payment-options UI users misread as loyalty-card-only. +6% credit card payments, complaints dropped to zero.

RETENTION-01.lever: Decouple a streak or habit-loop from hitting the full daily goal — let a smaller action (one lesson, one session) preserve it.
RETENTION-01.mechanism: Lowers the bar for the specific trigger that sustains the habit loop, without removing the goal itself.
RETENTION-01.condition: Churn is coming from missing an ambitious goal, not from lack of motivation to engage at all.
RETENTION-01.evidence: Duolingo: +40% increase in learners on a 7+ day streak.

RETENTION-02.lever: Show ambient social proof (real comments/reactions from other users) during use, not only at the payment moment.
RETENTION-02.mechanism: Doubt about whether the product is "working" creeps in mid-use, not just at checkout — proof needs to live where the doubt lives.
RETENTION-02.condition: Product is habit- or wellness-oriented, where the value is felt gradually rather than confirmed instantly.
RETENTION-02.evidence: Headspace: +3% survival rate of free trial users.

RETENTION-03.lever: Display concrete per-item numbers instead of only an aggregate total.
RETENTION-03.mechanism: An aggregate obscures the user's individual contribution; concrete numbers keep a recurring small habit legible over time.
RETENTION-03.condition: The habit involves recurring small actions (auto-invest, recurring workouts, recurring saves) where the total can hide whether it's still happening.
RETENTION-03.evidence: Stash: +12% of users still auto-investing 8 months later.

RETENTION-04.lever: Test icon/interaction choices (like/dislike, react, approve/reject) against the actual audience instead of assuming the more "appealing" icon wins.
RETENTION-04.mechanism: None assumed — this is the built-in reminder that icon aesthetics don't transfer across audiences.
RETENTION-04.condition: Any binary approve/reject or react UI. Always check_first for this category.
RETENTION-04.evidence: Paktor: thumbs up/down outperformed heart/X on clicks (+6%/+4.3%) and repeat usage (+2.3%) for this dating-app audience.

REFERRAL-01.lever: Show real-time visibility into a referral's progress (signup stages), not just success at the very end.
REFERRAL-01.mechanism: A black box between "invited" and "reward" kills motivation to keep tracking or pushing; visibility into "almost there" sustains it.
REFERRAL-01.condition: Referral rate is measurably low and the current flow only confirms success after the fact.
REFERRAL-01.evidence: SoFi: 20x increase in referrals, reaching 40% of new signups in 3 months.

REFERRAL-02.lever: Give referred users a longer trial than the standard new-user trial.
REFERRAL-02.mechanism: Referral programs need to convert skeptics who haven't yet decided the product is worth it, not just capture people who already had intent.
REFERRAL-02.condition: Referral flow currently gives referred users the same trial as everyone else.
REFERRAL-02.evidence: Headspace 30-Day Guest Pass: +7% new signups, +8% revenue from a higher free-to-paid conversion via referrals.

MONETIZE-01.lever: Add "Pro"/locked badges to premium-only features with no other change to the app.
MONETIZE-01.mechanism: Creates upgrade awareness without a hard wall — free users see what they're missing continuously instead of hitting it once.
MONETIZE-01.condition: Free users currently have no visible cue that a feature is premium-gated until they try to use it.

MONETIZE-02.lever: Gate the specific feature your most-engaged free users are already repeatedly hitting, identified from usage data — not an arbitrary feature.
MONETIZE-02.mechanism: Converts existing dependency into willingness to pay; gating a feature nobody uses converts nobody.
MONETIZE-02.condition: You have usage data showing which feature power users return to. The lift is specific to that segment, not the general free-user population.
MONETIZE-02.evidence: Busuu: +83% conversion among the power-user segment that hit the multi-language gate.

CTA-01.lever: Reframe CTA copy around the specific free-trial value ("Trial for free") instead of a generic action ("Sign up for free").
CTA-01.mechanism: Makes the free-trial angle explicit rather than implied.
CTA-01.condition: Audience already recognizes the brand/product; the CTA's job is to surface the trial angle, not explain the product.
CTA-01.evidence: Going: +104% trial starts month-over-month, also outperformed organic traffic for the first time.

CTA-02.lever: Show a monthly-equivalent price instead of the full lump-sum price.
CTA-02.mechanism: A lump sum reads as large; audiences that think in monthly-budget terms respond to the smaller framed number.
CTA-02.condition: Price is currently shown as a lump sum for a plan billed annually or in bulk.
CTA-02.evidence: Unacademy: +13.5% click-through rate at reported 100% significance.

CTA-03.lever: A visually distinctive button (e.g. thin border, standing apart from surrounding UI) can beat a button that blends into the existing design system.
CTA-03.mechanism: In a busy layout (carousel, dense list), visual distinctiveness competes for attention better than visual consistency.
CTA-03.condition: The CTA sits inside a crowded or scroll-heavy layout where it's competing with other content for attention.
CTA-03.evidence: Unacademy: the distinctive variant generated 13k clicks vs. 9k and 7k for the two more "on-brand" variants.

CTA-04.lever: Increase visual contrast between pricing tiers and emphasize the specific features customers say they value, rather than an even-handed feature list.
CTA-04.mechanism: A visually flat pricing table makes every tier look equally worth considering, which isn't decision-supporting.
CTA-04.condition: Multi-tier pricing page where tiers currently render with similar visual weight.
CTA-04.evidence: GitHub: +20% free and paid signups (bundled with color/cleanup changes, so this exact lift isn't isolated to contrast alone).

CTA-05.lever: "Simplify the page" is not a guaranteed win — verify with real data before assuming less is more.
CTA-05.mechanism: None assumed — this is the built-in caution rule for this category.
CTA-05.condition: Any time a simplification is proposed on the strength of intuition alone.
CTA-05.evidence: Instapage: the original, more detailed pricing page slightly outperformed the simplified variant (3.67% vs. 3.44%).
